content: For a gonococcal eye infection, administer a single dose of an appropriate antibiotic to treat the infection. Educate the mother on how to care for the baby’s eyes and schedule a follow-up visit in two days. If there is no improvement or the condition worsens, refer the baby urgently to a hospital. Additionally, assess and treat the mother and her partner for possible gonorrhea. For a local umbilical infection, teach the mother how to manage the infection. If there is no improvement within two days or if the condition worsens, refer the baby urgently to a hospital. For a local skin infection with fewer than 10 pustules, educate the mother on how to treat the infection. Schedule a follow-up in two days. If the pustules do not improve or worsen, refer the baby urgently to a hospital. If the baby exhibits danger signs, such as fast breathing (over 60 breaths per minute), slow or gasping breathing (less than 30 breaths per minute), severe chest in-drawing, poor feeding, grunting, convulsions, abdominal distension, cyanosis, a heart rate consistently over 180 beats per minute, or floppiness/stiffness, classify the condition as a possible serious illness. Administer the first dose of two intramuscular antibiotics and refer the baby urgently to a hospital. Advise against forcing the legs into a different position and handle any immobile limbs gently. If there is a malformation, refer the baby for specialized treatment and advise on surgical correction if necessary. Reassess after two feeds or one day. If the condition does not improve, teach her how to express milk from the affected breast and feed the baby by cup while continuing breastfeeding on the healthy side. For breast engorgement, encourage the mother to breastfeed more frequently and teach proper positioning and attachment. If the condition does not improve after two feeds or one day, teach her to express enough milk before feeding to relieve discomfort. For mastitis, where part of the breast is painful, swollen, and red, and the mother has a fever over 38°C, encourage her to continue breastfeeding and teach proper positioning and attachment. Prescribe a 10-day course of cloxacillin and reassess in two days. If there is no improvement or the condition worsens, refer her to a hospital. If the mother is HIV-positive, advise her to breastfeed on the healthy side and express and discard milk from the affected breast until the fever resolves. Support exclusive breastfeeding on demand, day and night, and assess breastfeeding before discharge. Teach the mother how to care for the baby, including keeping the baby warm, providing cord care, and maintaining hygiene. If the baby’s feet are cold, teach the mother to use skin-to-skin contact and reassess in one hour. If the baby has difficulty breathing, bleeding, or other abnormalities, examine the baby immediately and provide appropriate treatment. For small or preterm babies, plan to keep the baby longer before discharge and provide additional warmth and breastfeeding support. Encourage feeding every 2–3 hours and assess breastfeeding daily. If the baby is not feeding effectively, consider alternative feeding methods, such as expressing breast milk and cup feeding. If feeding difficulties persist for three days or the baby loses more than 10% of birth weight, refer for breastfeeding counseling and management. For replacement feeding, assess the mother’s feeding practices and teach her how to prepare and feed the baby using a cup. If the baby is not feeding well, refer urgently to a hospital. For breastfeeding counseling, emphasize the importance of exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months of life. Explain that breast milk contains all the nutrients a baby needs, is easily digested, and protects against infections. Encourage breastfeeding within one hour of birth and teach proper positioning and attachment. If the mother is unable to breastfeed, help her express milk and feed the baby by cup. For expressing breast milk, teach the mother how to do this herself using clean containers. If milk flow is poor, suggest warm compresses, back massage, or breast massage. If the baby is very small, teach the mother to express milk directly into the baby’s mouth or use heat-treated expressed milk if necessary. For cup feeding, teach the mother to hold the baby semi-upright and feed milk from a cup without pouring it into the baby’s mouth. For weight monitoring, weigh the baby daily if small or ill, and assess weight gain. A baby should lose no more than 10% of birth weight in the first week and gain at least 160 grams per week thereafter. Use a precise and accurate scale, calibrated daily. For mothers who are not breastfeeding, teach them how to relieve engorgement and provide alternative feeding options, such as donated heat-treated breast milk or formula, using a cup.
